text: Grace has three tenses: it appeared and saved you, it's teaching you now, and it keeps you looking for the blessed hope.
explanation:
"The grace of God that brings salvation has appeared to all men": that's the past, when Jesus was born, because grace isn't a doctrine but a Person. "Teaching us… we should live soberly, righteously, and godly in the present age": that's the present. "Looking for the blessed hope and glorious appearing of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ": that's the future.

The first two get preached often. The third is almost forgotten. Yet hope is what keeps a believer steady in an unsteady world. You were saved by grace, you're being taught by grace, and grace is carrying you toward His appearing.

text: It doesn't say you must teach people to deny ungodliness. It says grace teaches them.
explanation:
Many parents and leaders try to produce holiness by telling people what to do and not do. But most people already know what's right; they lack the power to do it. Paul says it's "the grace of God" that teaches us to deny ungodliness. Grace is a better teacher than you are.

A man struggling with drugs and alcohol for ten years said condemnation always drove him back to using. When he learned that God wasn't angry with him and his sins were forgiven, he went months clean, and kept going. Let grace flow, and the dead leaves fall off by themselves.

text: To create, God only had to speak. To redeem, He had to bleed.
explanation:
"By the word of the Lord the heavens were made." God spoke, and galaxies appeared. But not even God could simply wish away the consequences of sin. You can choose to put your finger in a fire, but you can't choose not to be burned; you can't choose the result of your choice.

God gave man a real choice, and man chose sin. The only way to undo its consequences was for Someone to bear them. So He gave His Son, "redeemed… with the precious blood of Christ." Creation cost Him a word. You cost Him His blood.

text: Paul calls your body "lowly." There's one gift still waiting for you: a body like Jesus' glorious body.
explanation:
"We eagerly wait for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body that it may be conformed to His glorious body." Your spirit is already new; your body is the last part of the inheritance Jesus bought, still to be delivered.

And look at His risen body: "Handle Me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see I have." He ate broiled fish in front of them. Yet He could appear in a locked room. You won't float around as a ghost. You'll have a real body that never tires, never ages and never dies.

text: When Moses delayed coming down the mountain, Israel made a golden calf. Forgetting that Jesus is coming produces the same drift.
explanation:
"When the people saw that Moses delayed coming down from the mountain," they said, "Come, make us gods." Jesus told of a servant who said in his heart, "My master is delaying his coming," and began to beat his fellow servants and live carelessly.

If He seems to be taking a long time, it's because "the Lord is not slack concerning His promise… not willing that any should perish." And John says, "Everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself." The blessed hope isn't escapism; it's what keeps you living for what lasts.

text: The "falling away" in 2 Thessalonians 2:3 is apostasia. Tyndale and the Geneva Bible both translated it "a departing."
explanation:
The Thessalonians had been shaken by reports that the day of the Lord had already come and they'd missed it. Paul wrote to calm them: "That Day will not come unless the apostasia comes first, and the man of sin is revealed." The word means departure: apo (from) and histemi (stand). It's used only one other time in the New Testament.

William Tyndale's 1526 New Testament and the Geneva Bible both render it "a departing first." Read that way, it's comfort, not threat: the church departs first, and only then is the lawless one revealed. Paul wasn't trying to frighten them; he was telling them not to be troubled.

text: Money can buy a bed, but not sleep. It can buy pills, but not peace.
explanation:
As a new year begins, many people pin their hopes on one more promotion or one more million, believing it'll finally make them happy. Some of the wealthiest people own houses they hardly live in and can't rest in any of them.

God isn't against you having money. "The blessing of the Lord makes one rich, and He adds no sorrow with it." But don't confuse more with happier. They say some people are so heavenly-minded they're no earthly good. In fact, the more heavenly-minded you are, the more earthly good you'll be: you hold things lightly, and you walk into a room like royalty.
